description:
Hi! I’m Charlen, from Huanuco. I love building interactive simulations that make engineering feel real, and I’ve worked on 3D simulators with three.js, gesture control with MediaPipe, and mobile apps for Android and iOS.

Our project is a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer: a game where students run a lunar station for 30 days, balancing power, life support, radiation shielding and food. Instead of moving sliders, you make concrete choices and see their effects inside the station.
summary: Lunar Station Commander is an interactive 3D educational simulation designed for the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players take command of a four-person lunar habitat for 30 days, managing shared electricity, oxygen, food, and crew health while following a daily routine modeled after the International Space Station (ISS).   The simulator addresses the challenge by turning complex spaceflight survival trade-offs into accessible, hands-on decision-making for youth. Every choice carries real consequences: solar panels generate power only during lunar daylight, night operations drain battery reserves, and incoming solar storms—announced two days in advance—require reinforcing radiation shielding or taking shelter. Powered by real NASA datasets (DONKI space weather, OSDR human biology, and RadLab dosimetry) alongside Canadian Space Agency (CSA) lunar agriculture guides, the platform includes trilingual support (English, Spanish, and Portuguese) and optional webcam motion tracking. It empowers students worldwide to experience the science, resource management, and resilience required for sustainable lunar exploration.
details:
Lunar Station Commander places students in the role of mission commander aboard a closed-loop lunar habitat for a 30-day mission with a crew of four. Because nobody can survive outside the habitat, every system shares a single electrical grid where allocating resources to one subsystem directly impacts another. Players progress through an ISS-inspired daily cycle—waking up, eating three meals, completing morning and afternoon operational tasks, exercising on a treadmill to prevent muscle and bone loss, tending the lunar greenhouse, and sleeping. During critical turns, the onboard computer prompts players with engineering trade-offs (such as cranking solar panels for extra daytime power at the cost of crew oxygen, running fuel cells at night, or activating power-saving mode). Additionally, players receive a 2-day warning before solar storms hit, requiring timely habitat shielding and hatch closure.

Benefits & Intended Impact By replacing passive reading with active cause-and-effect simulation, the trainer builds STEM literacy, critical thinking, and systems-engineering awareness among young learners. Built-in support for English, Spanish, and Portuguese removes language barriers for students across the Americas and beyond.

Tools, Technologies & Accessibility

  • Frontend & 3D Engine: Built for the web using HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and Three.js / WebGL for real-time 3D rendering of the lunar surface, habitat modules, greenhouse, and crew.
  • Controls & Accessibility: Supports mouse, touch, keyboard shortcuts (keys 1–5 and WASD/arrows), and webcam-based computer vision/motion tracking so students can control their astronaut's arms and movement hands-free.

Creativity & Design Considerations Our team focused on balancing scientific authenticity with intuitive game mechanics: integrating lunar day/night power cycles, real radiation risk windows, closed-loop food production, and physical fitness routinesinto a clear visual HUD displaying real-time time progression and vital metrics (Oxygen, Food, Battery, and Crew Health).
